blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Recovering 3D pose and shape of birds from single images is bottlenecked by the long tail of avian diversity: out of ~10,000 species, only a few dozen have 3D-labeled training data, and in-the-wild test sets routinely contain species never seen at training. Generalizing across clades is therefore a central problem. The current state of the art, AniMer+, mitigates it with a family-level contrastive loss that conveys only a binary same-family indicator per pair and discards the continuous structure of the species tree. We propose a taxonomic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck prior on the shape code of the AVES parametric bird mesh model: a multivariate Gaussian whose covariance decays exponentially with Linnaean rank distance, with a learnable selection strength and noise scale. The prior generalizes family contrastive into a continuous, generative form, exposing the graded cross- and within-family similarity that a binary indicator cannot, and brings continuous comparative phylogenetics in as a biology-grounded inductive bias for the long tail. Our method improves over AniMer+ on both metrics of the unseen-species CowBird benchmark and on CtrlAVES3D, while remaining comparable on seen-species CUB. A permutation ablation isolates taxonomic structure from generic Gaussian smoothing, and a rank-granularity ablation identifies cross-order distinctions (the structure beyond a family-vs-not indicator) as the dominant source of the unseen-species gain.

blocks.en:
Single-image articulated 3D reconstruction has progressed rapidly for
animals, from species-agnostic fits of the Skinned Multi-Animal Linear
(SMAL) model [ 3 ] to breed-aware
priors [ 4 ] , web-scale category models [ 5 ] , and
most recently to family-aware mixture-of-experts transformers for joint
mammal–bird recovery [ 1 ] . Birds, however, sharpen the
classical long-tail problem to an extreme. The world hosts on the order of 10 000 10\,000 extant bird species, yet 3D-labeled training data exist for only
a few dozen, and important in-the-wild benchmarks
(e.g. CowBird [ 6 ] ) contain species never seen at
training. A practical estimator must therefore
generalize across species: not just to new individuals or new poses, but to
new clades (groups of species sharing a common ancestor) whose body
plans the model has never been supervised on.
Bridging this gap requires a regularizer that injects prior
knowledge about how shape varies across species, knowledge that exists
abundantly in evolutionary biology but is not currently exploited by
single-view recovery pipelines.

blocks.en:
Parametric mesh models—SMAL [ 3 ] (a multi-animal extension of SMPL [ 14 ] ) for quadrupeds and AVES [ 12 ] for birds—are the dominant approach for animal 3D reconstruction. Category-specific mesh reconstruction [ 15 ] and wild-animal fitting [ 16 , 17 ] established the learning-based paradigm. Single-image regressors have since evolved from early
bird-specific reconstruction [ 6 ] through breed-aware
(BARC [ 4 ] ) and mixture-of-Gaussians (WLDO [ 18 ] )
shape priors to category-level (MagicPony [ 19 ] ) and
pan-category (3D-Fauna [ 5 ] ) models. For birds,
AniMer+ [ 1 ] (extending the mammal-only
AniMer [ 20 ] ) is the current state of the art: a
family-aware mixture-of-experts [ 21 ] transformer [ 22 ] trained jointly on mammals and
birds with a family-level supervised-contrastive [ 7 ] ℒ con \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{con}} term. We keep the
AniMer+ backbone but replace the discrete ℒ con \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{con}} used by AniMer+ with a continuous rank-structured
generative prior, and show that continuous taxonomic structure
matters, both theoretically and empirically. ℒ con \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{con}} is the structural analogue of our prior in
the degenerate α → ∞ \alpha\!\to\!\infty case ( Section 3.4 ),
and a controlled permutation ablation tests the taxonomic content.

blocks.en:
Hierarchical classification [ 23 , 24 ] embeds
class-level structure into learning objectives, and image-based methods
exploit taxonomy discretely, including the breed triplet loss of
BARC [ 4 ] and the family-level supervised
contrastive [ 7 ] loss of AniMer+; the latter two are
pair losses with a 1-bit-per-pair information budget. Such losses can
be read as implicit class-conditional Gaussians with a block-diagonal covariance (one
block per family). The OU [ 10 ] process as a model
of continuous trait evolution on a tree is classical in phylogenetic
comparative methods [ 25 , 8 , 9 ] ;
tree-structured OU priors have appeared in
Draupnir [ 26 ] , a VAE for ancestral protein sequences,
but to our knowledge not in 3D articulated shape estimation. Our prior
replaces the block-diagonal with a dense, rank-structured Σ \Sigma indexed by a Linnaean [ 2 ] rank distance,
retaining the discrete class-block as the α → ∞ \alpha\!\to\!\infty degenerate case ( Section 3.4 ).

blocks.en: 3.1 Preliminaries: OU process and taxonomic distance
blocks.zh: 3.1 初步情况: OU 过程和分类距离

blocks.en:
Closely related species tend to have similar body shapes, and the
similarity fades as the relationship becomes more distant. An OU
process is a standard model in comparative phylogenetics for a
continuous trait that evolves along a species tree while being
pulled toward an optimum; under it the trait values of two species
are correlated, and the correlation decays exponentially with their
distance on the tree. The Linnaean rank distance supplies that
distance from standard taxonomy alone, as a small integer that grows
as the pair’s shared group moves up from species to family, order,
and beyond. The resulting covariance matrix over species is the
Gaussian prior we place on the AVES shape code.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We introduced a taxonomic Ornstein–Uhlenbeck [ 10 ] prior on the AVES [ 12 ] shape code for single-view avian
3D shape recovery. The prior generalizes the family supervised
contrastive [ 7 ] signal used by the prior state of the
art [ 1 ] into a continuous, generative form indexed
by a Linnaean [ 2 ] rank distance matrix, supplying
graded cross-species similarity that a binary same-family indicator
cannot represent. As a unit, the proposed
method improves over the prior state of the art on both metrics of the
unseen-species CowBird benchmark and on CtrlAVES3D while remaining
comparable on seen-species CUB, isolates the contribution of taxonomic
structure from generic Gaussian smoothing through a controlled
permutation ablation, and identifies cross-order rank distinctions,
the information that lies beyond a family-vs-not indicator, as the
dominant source of the unseen-species gain. Taken together, the
experiments support a biology-grounded inductive bias for long-tailed
avian shape recovery.

The prior is evaluated on a 17 17 -species training taxonomy with
limited within-order density and no congeneric pair, so genus-level
structure is untested, and the unseen-species benchmark,
CowBird [ 6 ] , covers a single species. The rank matrix D tax D_{\mathrm{tax}} follows a single taxonomic
authority [ 2 ] ; we have not tested robustness to
competing resolutions of contested inter-order relationships, and
larger-scale use should regenerate the matrix as taxonomic consensus
evolves. The OU formulation is
not bird-specific, but extending it to other animal groups requires a
compatible parametric shape model, taxonomic annotations and
3D-labeled data, and how the gains behave at hundreds or thousands
of species remains to be established.

blocks.en: Appendix S10 Extended discussion: limitations and future work

blocks.en: This appendix expands on the limitations and future directions summarized at the end of Section 5 , and lays out the three follow-up directions we see as most natural: lifting the pipeline to multi-view 3D reconstruction, replacing the discrete Linnaean rank distance with a continuous molecular phylogeny, and porting the same OU machinery to mammals. Each direction adds exactly one ingredient to the present setup – multiple views, a continuous tree, or a non-avian dataset – while leaving the OU prior itself unchanged. We discuss each in turn, together with the obstacles a follow-up paper would need to address.

head as a per-Gaussian regressor, which we leave as future work.

code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main

operating point and Table S6 the per-trial values;
